faq.q: What is the diaphragm in a microphone?
faq.a: It is a very thin, light sheet of plastic or metal foil. Sound waves push and pull it, so it vibrates in exactly the same pattern as the sound.

faq.q: How does a dynamic microphone make electricity?
faq.a: A small coil is attached to the diaphragm and sits around a magnet. As the coil moves back and forth, the changing magnetic field induces a tiny current in it.
asks: Why does a moving coil make a current?

faq.q: How does the current carry the sound?
faq.a: The current rises and falls exactly in step with the air pressure. Loud sounds make a bigger current and high notes make it wobble faster, so the signal is a copy of the sound.
asks: How does a microphone signal match my voice?

faq.q: Why does a microphone need an amplifier?
faq.a: A microphone's signal is tiny, only thousandths of a volt. An amplifier boosts it so it can be recorded, sent to a speaker or turned into numbers by a computer.
asks: Why is a microphone signal so weak?

faq.q: Is a microphone like a speaker backwards?
faq.a: A dynamic microphone is: in a speaker, current moves a coil to push air; in a microphone, air moves a coil to make current. Phones mostly use tiny condenser microphones, which sense the diaphragm moving near a charged plate.
asks: How does a phone microphone work?

facts: A dynamic microphone typically gives only a few thousandths of a volt.
Most phone microphones are tiny condenser microphones built on silicon chips, called MEMS microphones.

quiz.why: The sound moves the diaphragm and its coil past a magnet, and the changing field induces a current.
